transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 09:30 PST | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Nina (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Hannah (CSM), Ravi (CTO, Quantaco AI), Sara (ML Eng), Luis (FinOps), Maya (Product)

Summary: quick recap of last week's benchmark, deep dive on tokens/sec/$, caching savings from prefix/KV cache, and batching tradeoffs. Agree to run a larger weekend run and share an updated cost model.

Topics: cost per token, tokens per second per GPU, caching & KV cash savings, batch sizing vs p99 latency, quantization profiles (int8/int4), Dedicated routing and fallback.

00:00 Nina: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um quick agenda — run through the numbers we pulled last week, discuss tuning, and agree next steps.
00:12 Ravi: yeah thanks, this is Ravi. excited to see the cost side, we've been comparing this to Anthropic and OpenAI costs.
00:20 Marcus: cool, i'll start with the benchmark recap — last run was 50k tokens across a mix of short and long sequences; avg token/sec on the 80A GPU was ~3,200 tokens/sec and cost came out to about $0.0045 per 1k tokens after batching and our cache hits. those numbers are approximate, transcription may flip some numbers.
00:43 Sara: wait when you say cache hits, is that prefix caching or KV? we're using a lot of short prompts with user history so prefix cache would matter a lot.
00:52 Marcus: good question — mostly prefix + KV caching, though our export labelled it KV "cash" in some places so ignore that typo. effective cache hit rate was ~28% across the mix which reduced generated tokens by roughly 20%.
01:10 Luis: and that 20% reduction translated directly to cost savings? curious how you attribute the savings between batching and caching.
01:18 Marcus: right — so two levers: caching reduces the number of tokens we actually need to generate; batching increases tokens/sec and amortizes fixed costs (kernel launch, 1st token overhead). in our run caching shaved ~20% off cost, batching improvements (moving from batch size 1 to 8) dropped cost per token by an additional ~35% but increased p99 latency from ~220ms to ~520ms for the long-tail.
01:44 Maya: ok that's the tradeoff we expected. for product we care about p95 latency under 300ms for interactive features; p99 can be higher for background jobs.
01:54 Nina: exactly — that's why we want to show both tokens/sec/$ and the latency distribution. Luis, for FinOps, what's your target tokens per dollar?
02:02 Luis: ballpark we want at least 200k tokens per dollar for the pilot, ideally 300k if quality holds.
02:09 Marcus: current runs are at roughly 222k tokens per dollar on the int8 profile with caching and batching of 8, so we are in the ballpark. if we move to int4 we see higher throughput but some quality drop depending on model and quantization knobs.
02:24 Sara: do you have per-model breakdowns? we're testing t5-like small models and a 30B variant — quantization effects differ.
02:31 Marcus: yes — for the 30B variant int8 gave ~3,200 tok/sec; int4 pushed to ~4,700 tok/sec but hallucination risk and slight rouge/perf drop on our eval set. i'll add per-model RBC (that's RBC? i mean RCE, ha) in the spreadsheet.
02:52 Ravi: can you explain the tokens/sec/$ calc again, i want to make sure i'm reading the sheet right.
02:58 Marcus: sure — simple: (tokens_generated_total) / (cost_of_run). cost includes GPU runtime + infra overhead + egress (where applicable). we normalize to tokens per dollar. batching increases tokens_generated per second so the numerator improves; caching reduces tokens_generated_total so it lowers numerator but also lowers cost because run duration shrinks. net effect depends on cache hit mix.
03:20 Nina: we also experimented with Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity for consistent throughput — that lowers unit GPU cost vs on-demand so tokens/$ improves if you commit.
03:30 Luis: what's the math on that? how much improvement with reserved?
03:34 Marcus: in our pricing assumptions, a reserved Dedicated pool reduces effective GPU cost by ~18-25% depending on commit term and burst behavior. that moves the 222k tokens/$ up to ~270-280k tokens/$ for the same perf profile.
03:50 Sara: are there any hidden costs when you scale batching? memory or kv cache size limits or kernel fallbacks?
03:57 Marcus: yes — bigger batches push memory pressure, can increase KV cache misses if you need more prefixes in memory; and for some attention kernels the scheduling can change which affects p99. we saw a kernel fallback in one run under extreme long context which spiked latency.
04:15 Ravi: hmm ok, so practical recommendation — keep batching moderate for interactive paths and allow higher batch for async/background.
04:23 Marcus: yes, and we can route requests by policy: low-latency route with batch size 2-4, and high-throughput route with batch 16+. Redwood's routing can fallback to a cheaper model variant if capacity constrained; that helps cost while controlling p99.
04:40 Luis: do you have numbers for mixed traffic? like 80/20 interactive vs background?
04:47 Marcus: we ran a synthetic mix — with 80% interactive (batch 2) and 20% background (batch 16) the blended tokens/$ was roughly 240k tokens/$ and p95 stayed under 280ms. that's promising but depends on actual traffic shape.
05:05 Sara: about caching — you mentioned 28% hit. how do we increase that? more prefix canonicalization or session affinity?
05:12 Marcus: both. canonicalizing prompts (normalize dates, strip ephemeral ids), using session affinity to hit cached prefixes, and TTL tuning on KV cache. we can also cache more aggressively on the client side for repeated system prompts.
05:28 Ravi: any security concerns with caching? our data includes some PII in conversation history.
05:33 Nina: yep we flagged that — Redwood's KV cache can be configured to not persist PII and to encrypt at rest; for Private deployments we can run cache in-customer VPC. Marcus will attach security doc snippets.
05:46 Hannah: adding — we'll include SOC 2 and KMS integration notes in the emailed security pack.
05:54 Luis: ok good. on cost model spreadsheet — please include scenario columns: hosted on-demand, dedicated reserved 6mo, dedicated reserved 12mo, and private op-ex. that helps procurement.
06:06 Nina: will do. Marcus, can you walk through the sample rows in the spreadsheet now?
06:11 Marcus: sure — open link, first row is baseline: on-demand single-GPU with batch 1, no caching. tokens/$ there is low: ~70k tokens/$. row two applies batching and caching - see tokens/$ jump. row three is reserved Dedicated int8 with batch 8 and 28% cache — that's the 222k tokens/$.
06:32 Maya: what's the sensitivity to cache hit rate — a chart would help.
06:36 Marcus: yep — quick note: at 10% cache hit tokens/$ ~190k, at 28% ~222k, at 45% ~270k. it's non-linear because background run durations shrink and you get more efficient batching.
06:52 Ravi: great. any competitor comparison we should be aware of?
06:55 Marcus: high level: OpenAI's hosted tends to have lower latency but higher $/token for large contexts; Anthropic numbers are competitive on safety but cost varies. Vertex/managed endpoints give control but you need to manage batching + autoscale. we'll put a competitor slide in the follow-up pack.
07:13 Luis: what about egress and multi-region—we have users in EU and NA. does multi-region increase cost materially?
07:20 Marcus: yes egress and cross-region replication of cache adds cost; routing by region to avoid cross-region egress is best. Redwood supports region routing and will fall back to nearest region if capacity constrained. that said, if you need private connectivity (VPC), there's op-ex for that.
07:34 Sara: any notes on model flavoring — i.e. cheaper smaller model for low-criticality responses and larger for important ones?
07:40 Marcus: yes model routing policy can send low-criticality queries to a 7B or 13B variant and high-criticality to 30B; ensemble fallback if quality dips. that boosts tokens/$.
07:52 Nina: ok let's surface a concrete ask — Marcus, can you run a weekend run 100k tokens, 8k context, compare int8 vs int4 vs int4+mix, and measure tokens/ $ + p95/p99 latencies?
07:06 Marcus: yes i'll run that and include kernel-level logs where we saw fallsback.
08:12 Sara: one more question — does Redwood's caching handle partial prefix matches? our dialogues often share partial sequences.
08:20 Marcus: we support longest-prefix match; partial match caching hits are lower but canonicalization can improve that.
08:30 Luis: ok great. procurement side — if we opt for Dedicated, how fast is capacity provisioning?
08:36 Nina: typical lead times are 2-3 weeks for Dedicated pools depending on region; we can use hosted as a bridge.
08:43 Ravi: good. any blockers from our side? Sara: we need to validate quality after int4 runs; we want a quick eval script.
08:51 Marcus: i'll include the eval harness and rouge/semantic similarity metrics we used. note that int4 needs per-layer calibration for some weights, so quality varies.
09:05 Maya: can you also show cost per 1M tokens as a simple number for stakeholder slide?
09:09 Marcus: sure — on current reserved int8 config it's ~ $3.7 per 1M tokens (approx). on int4 reserved it drops to ~ $2.4 per 1M tokens but with caveats on quality.
09:24 Luis: that's useful. ok i'm comfortable proceeding with the weekend benchmark and the spreadsheet.
09:28 Nina: sweet, we'll send notes and security pack by EOD. thanks everyone.
09:34 Ravi: thanks.
09:36 Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: automatic transcript with some mishears (cash vs cache, RBC -> RCE). timestamps approximate.
